The '''bitter orange''', '''sour orange''', '''Seville orange''', '''bigarade orange''', or '''marmalade orange''' is the hybrid [[citrus]] tree species '''''Citrus'' × ''aurantium''''', and its fruit. It is native to [[Southeast Asia]] and has been spread by humans to many parts of the world. It is a cross between the pomelo, ''[[Citrus maxima]]'', and the wild type mandarin orange, ''[[Citrus reticulata]]''. The bitter orange is used to make [[essential oil]], used in foods, drinks, and pharmaceuticals. The Seville orange is prized for making British orange [[marmalade]].

== Definition ==

In some proposed systems, the species ''Citrus'' × ''aurantium'' includes not only the bitter orange proper, but all other [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]]s between the [[pomelo]] and the wild type [[mandarin orange|mandarin]], namely the [[sweet orange]], the [[grapefruit]], and all cultivated [[mandarin orange|mandarins]].<ref name="Talon 2020">{{cite book |last1=Talon |first1=M. |last2=Caruso |first2=M. |last3=Gmitter |first3=F.G. |title=The Genus Citrus |publisher=[[Elsevier Science]] |year=2020 |isbn=978-0-12-812217-4}} p. 69–70</ref><ref name="Mabberley 2022">{{cite journal |last=Mabberley |first=David J. |date=6 September 2022 |title=A classification for edible citrus: an update, with a note on Murraya (Rutaceae) |journal= Telopea|volume=25 |pages=271–284 |doi=10.7751/telopea15954 |bibcode=2022Telop..2515954M |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Powo">{{cite web |title=''Citrus'' × ''aurantium'' L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:59600-2 |website=Plants of the World Online |access-date=17 April 2023 |archive-date=27 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230327112733/https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:59600-2 |url-status=live }}</ref> This article only deals with the bitter orange proper.

== History ==

{{see also|Citrus taxonomy}}

The bitter orange, like many cultivated ''[[Citrus]]'' species, is a hybrid, in its case of the wild [[Mandarin orange|mandarin]] and [[pomelo]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Klein |first1=Joshua D. |volume=2 |pages=199–214 |doi=10.1007/978-94-017-9276-9_10 |series=Medicinal and Aromatic Plants of the World |year=2014 |title=Medicinal and Aromatic Plants of the Middle-East |isbn=978-94-017-9275-2 |chapter=Citron Cultivation, Production and Uses in the Mediterranean Region}}</ref><ref name="Wu Terol Ibanez 2018">{{cite journal |last1=Wu |first1=Guohong Albert |last2=Terol |first2=Javier |last3=Ibanez |first3=Victoria |last4=López-García |first4=Antonio |last5=Pérez-Román |first5=Estela |last6=Borredá |first6=Carles |last7=Domingo |first7=Concha |last8=Tadeo |first8=Francisco R. |last9=Carbonell-Caballero |first9=Jose |last10=Alonso |first10=Roberto |last11=Curk |first11=Franck |last12=Du |first12=Dongliang |last13=Ollitrault |first13=Patrick |last14=Roose |first14=Mikeal L. == Botany ==

=== Description ===

[[File:Citrus aurantium - Köhler–s Medizinal-Pflanzen-042.jpg|thumb|Foliage, blossoms and fruit. ''Köhler's Medizinal-Pflanzen'', 1897]]

The bitter orange has orange fruit with a distinctly bitter or sour taste. The tree has alternate simple leaves on long [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]]; there are long thorns on the petiole. The trees require little care and may live for as long as 600 years. It grows in subtropical regions but can tolerate a brief frost.<ref name=purdue/>

=== Pests and diseases ===

The bitter orange has many of the same pests and diseases as other citrus fruits. Viral diseases include [[citrus tristeza virus]], [[Citrus variegation virus|crinkly leaf virus]], and [[Citrus chachexia viroid|xyloporosis]]. Among the many fungal diseases are [[anthracnose]], [[Diaporthe citri|dieback]], and [[heart rot]].<ref name=purdue/>

=== Varieties ===

{{See also|Citrus taxonomy#Oranges}}

* ''C.'' × ''aurantium'' var. ''myrtifolia'' is possibly a distinct species, ''[[Citrus myrtifolia]]''. The '[[Chinotto]]' cultivar is used to make the [[Chinotto (drink)|drink of the same name]].<ref>{{cite web |title=The cult of Chinotto, Italy's national soda |url=https://www.thegrandwinetour.com/en/favorite-italian-wines/chinotto-italys-national-soda |website=The Grand Wine Tour |access-date=3 January 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201109040518/https://www.thegrandwinetour.com/en/favorite-italian-wines/chinotto-italys-national-soda |archive-date=9 November 2020 |date=4 June 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* ''C.'' × ''aurantium'' var. ''daidai'', the [[daidai]], is used in [[Traditional Chinese medicine|Chinese medicine]] and in tea.<ref name=purdue/>
* ''C.'' × ''aurantium'' subsp. ''currassuviencis'', the [[laraha]], grows on the [[Caribbean]] island of Curaçao. The dried peel is used in [[Curaçao (liqueur)|Curaçao liqueur]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Curacao |url=https://www.food.com/about/curacao-432 |website=Food.com |access-date=4 November 2024 |archive-date=28 February 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150228123727/https://www.food.com/about/curacao-432 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Among the many related species is ''Citrus bergamia'', the [[bergamot orange]]. This is probably a bitter orange and [[limetta]] hybrid; it is cultivated in Italy for the production of bergamot oil, a component of many brands of [[perfume]] and tea, especially [[Earl Grey tea]].<ref>{{GRIN |''Citrus bergamia'' |10698 |access-date = 2017-12-12}}</ref> It is a less hardy plant than other bitter orange varieties.<ref name=purdue/>

== Uses ==

=== Culinary ===

While the raw pulp is not usually eaten,<ref>{{cite book |last=Little |first=Elbert L. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Western Region |year=1994 |orig-year=1980 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=0394507614 |edition=Chanticleer Press |page=510}}</ref> bitter orange is widely used in cooking. The Seville orange (the usual name in this context) is prized for making British orange [[marmalade]], being higher in [[pectin]] than the [[orange (fruit)|sweet orange]], and therefore giving a better set and a higher yield. Once a year, oranges of this variety are collected from trees in [[Seville]] and shipped to [[United Kingdom|Britain]] to be used in marmalade. However, the fruit is rarely consumed locally in [[Andalusia]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Ortega |first=Cristina |url=http://www.20minutos.es/noticia/193691/0/aprovechara/naranja/capital/ |title=Apenas se aprovechará la naranja que se recoja en la capital este año |website=20minutos Sevilla |date=22 January 2007 |access-date=3 November 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110511210751/https://www.20minutos.es/noticia/193691/0/aprovechara/naranja/capital/ |archive-date=11 May 2011 |url-status=live}}</ref> This reflects Britain, Portugal and Spain's historic [[Atlantic World|Atlantic trading relationship]]; an early recipe for 'marmelet of oranges' was recorded by Eliza Cholmondeley in 1677<!--in Cheshire, in her ''Book of Receipts''-->.<ref>{{cite web |title=20 fascinating facts about marmalade |url=https://www.countrylife.co.uk/food-drink/20-fascinating-facts-about-marmalade-69672 |publisher=[[Country Life (magazine)|Country Life]] |access-date=2 November 2024 |date=27 February 2015 |archive-date=25 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240725065003/https://www.countrylife.co.uk/food-drink/20-fascinating-facts-about-marmalade-69672 |url-status=live }}</ref> Bitter orange—''bigarade''—was used in all early recipes for ''[[duck à l'orange]]'', originally called ''canard à la bigarade''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Ude |first=Louis Eustache |title=The French Cook |publisher=John Ebers |location=London |edition=6th |year=1819 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8pbRRljMY_0C&q=ducklings%20%20bigarade&pg=PA212 |page=212}}</ref> [[Malta]] too has a tradition of making bitter oranges into marmalade.<ref>{{Cite web |last=MCA |date=2021-04-19 |title=Orange Marmalade |url=https://www.mcamalta.com/post/orange-marmalade |access-date=2022-07-19 |website=MCA Malta |language=en |archive-date=2022-05-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220516194553/https://www.mcamalta.com/post/orange-marmalade |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-05-03 |title=Ċitru f'Malta |url=https://agrikoltura.wordpress.com/2021/05/03/citru-fmalta/ |access-date=2022-07-19 |website=Dilettanti tal-Agrikoltura Siġar u Pjanti |language=en |archive-date=2022-07-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220719140721/https://agrikoltura.wordpress.com/2021/05/03/citru-fmalta/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In Finland, [[mämmi]] is a fermented malted rye dough flavoured with ground Seville orange zest.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.dlc.fi/~marianna/gourmet/mammi.htm | title=Mämmi | work=Nordic Recipe Archive | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221221045601/http://www.dlc.fi/~marianna/gourmet/mammi.htm | archive-date=2022-12-21 | url-status=dead}}</ref>
Across Scandinavia, bitter orange peel is used in dried, ground form in baked goods such as Christmas bread<ref>{{cite web |title=Pomeransbröd |url=https://www.koket.se/pomeransbrod |website=Köket.se |access-date=3 November 2024 |language=sv}}</ref> and gingerbread.<ref>{{cite news |title=Skurna pepparkakor med mandel och pomerans |url=https://www.dn.se/mat-dryck/recept/skurna-pepparkakor-med-mandel-och-pomerans/ |access-date=3 November 2024 |work=[[Dagens Nyheter]] |date=28 November 2015 |language=sv |archive-date=4 August 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250804063436/https://www.dn.se/mat-dryck/recept/skurna-pepparkakor-med-mandel-och-pomerans/ |url-status=live }}</ref> 
In [[Greece]], the ''nerántzi'' is one of the most prized fruits used for [[spoon sweets]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Gogos |first=Dora Kitinas |title=Glyko tou koutaliou (spoon sweets) |url=https://neoskosmos.com/en/2012/07/04/life/food-drink/glyko-tou-koutaliou/ |publisher=Neos Kosmos |access-date=3 November 2024 |date=4 July 2012 |archive-date=4 December 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241204021533/https://neoskosmos.com/en/2012/07/04/life/food-drink/glyko-tou-koutaliou/ |url-status=live }}</ref> 
In Adana province, [[Turkish cuisine|Turkey]], bitter orange jam is a principal dessert.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Guzeler |first1=Nuray |last2=Yildirim |first2=Cagla |last3=Aridici |first3=Ayse |title=The Culinary Culture and Traditional Foods of Adana Province |journal=Journal of Agricultural Faculty of Uludag University |date=2016 |volume=30 |issue=Special Issue |pages=538–545 |url=https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/pdf/10.5555/20173246120}}</ref> 
Bitter oranges are made into [[chutney]]s in India, either in the style of a [[raita]] with curds, or roasted, spiced, and sweetened to form a condiment that can be preserved in jars.<ref>{{cite web |last=Mandanna |first=Sharada |title=Bitter Orange Chutney |url=https://www.coorgtourisminfo.com/recipie/bitter-orange-chutney-by-sharada-mandanna/ |publisher=Coorg Tourism Info |access-date=3 November 2024 |archive-date=4 December 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241204021907/https://www.coorgtourisminfo.com/recipie/bitter-orange-chutney-by-sharada-mandanna/ |url-status=live }}</ref> 
In Yucatán (Mexico), it is a main ingredient of the ''[[cochinita pibil]]''.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kennedy |first1=Diana |last2=Presilla |first2=Maricel E. |last3=Rao |first3=Tejal |title=Cochinita Pibil |url=https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/1018283-cochinita-pibil |publisher=New York Times Cooking |access-date=3 November 2024 |archive-date=28 September 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240928023600/https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/1018283-cochinita-pibil |url-status=live }}</ref> 
In [[Suriname]], its juice is used in the well-known dish [[Pom (dish)|pom]].<ref name="Vaneker 2012">{{cite book | last=Vaneker | first=Karin | title=Reimagining Marginalized Foods | chapter=Discovering Pom’s Potential | publisher=[[University of Arizona Press]] | date=1 November 2012 | doi=10.2307/j.ctt1814g4b.8 |doi-access=free | pages=88–108 |jstor=j.ctt1814g4b.8| isbn=978-0-8165-0236-3 }}</ref>

An [[essential oil]] is extracted from the peel of dried, unripe bitter oranges; ''C. aurantium'' var. ''curassaviensis'' in particular is used in [[Curaçao (liqueur)|Curaçao liqueur]].<ref name=purdue/> An oil is pressed from the fresh peel of ripe fruit in many countries and used in ice creams, puddings, sweets, soft and alcoholic drinks, and pharmaceuticals.<ref name=purdue/> The flowers are distilled to yield [[Neroli]] oil<ref name=purdue/> and [[orange flower water]],<ref name="Duffy 2005">{{cite news |last1=Duffy |first1=Nikki |title=Super Ingredients: Orange Flower Water |url=https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2005/jul/09/foodanddrink.shopping3 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=9 July 2005}}</ref> with similar uses.<ref name=purdue/> Neroli oil is also employed in [[perfume]]s.<ref>{{cite book |last=Arctander |first=Steffen |date=1960 |title=Perfume and Flavor Materials of Natural Origin |page=436 |publisher=Orchard Innovations |isbn=195168205X}}</ref> 
The peel of bitter oranges is used as a spice in Belgian ''[[Witbier]]'' (white [[beer]]), for orange-flavored liqueurs such as [[Cointreau]], and to produce [[bitters]] such as [[Orange bitters|Oranjebitter]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Bitter Orange or Seville Orange |url=https://www.botanischetuinen.nl/en/plant_en/2622/bitter-orange-or-seville-orange |website=Botanic Guardians |access-date=3 November 2024}}</ref> It is a component of Nordic hot spiced wine, ''[[glögg]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=Swedish Christmas Glögg |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/food/recipes/annikas_glgg_annikas_32356 |publisher=BBC Food |access-date=3 November 2024}}</ref>

=== Rootstock, wood, and soap ===

The bitter orange is used as a [[rootstock]] in groves of sweet orange.<ref name=purdue/> The fruit and leaves make [[Foam|lather]] and can be used as [[soap]].<ref name=purdue/> The hard, white or light-yellow [[wood]] is used in [[woodworking]] and made into [[baseball bat]]s in Cuba.<ref name=purdue/>

=== Herbal stimulant ===

[[Solvent extraction|Extracts]] of bitter orange and its peel have been marketed as [[dietary supplement]]s purported to act as a weight-loss aid and [[appetite suppressant]].<ref name="sharpe">{{cite journal |last1=Sharpe |first1=Patricia A. |last2=Granner |first2=Michelle L. |last3=Conway |first3=Joan M. |last4=Ainsworth |first4=Barbara E. |last5=Dobre |first5=Mirela |title=Availability of weight-loss supplements: Results of an audit of retail outlets in a southeastern city |journal=Journal of the American Dietetic Association |volume=106 |issue=12 |pages=2045–51 |date=December 2006 |pmid=17126636 |doi=10.1016/j.jada.2006.09.014}}</ref><ref name="nccam"/> Bitter orange contains the [[tyramine]] metabolites [[N-Methyltyramine|''N''-methyltyramine]], [[octopamine (drug)|octopamine]], and [[synephrine]],<ref name="pmid18700609"/> substances similar to [[epinephrine]], which act on the [[alpha-1 adrenergic receptor|α<sub>1</sub> adrenergic receptor]] to [[vasoconstriction|constrict blood vessels]] and increase [[blood pressure]] and [[heart rate]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bui |first1=Linda T. |last2=Nguyen |first2=DiemThuy T. |last3=Ambrose |first3=Peter J. |title=Blood pressure and heart rate effects following a single dose of bitter orange |journal=[[The Annals of Pharmacotherapy]] |volume=40 |issue=1 |pages=53–7 |date=January 2006 |pmid=16317106 |doi=10.1345/aph.1G488 |s2cid=19625077}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hess |first1=A.M. |last2=Sullivan |first2=D.L. |title=Potential for toxicity with use of bitter orange extract and guarana for weight loss |journal=The Annals of Pharmacotherapy |volume=39 |issue=3 |pages=574–5 |date=March 2005 |pmid=15657116 |doi=10.1345/aph.1E249 |s2cid=28294405}}</ref>

Following bans on the herbal stimulant [[Ephedra (plant)|ephedra]] in the [[United States|U.S.]], [[Canada]], and elsewhere, bitter orange has been substituted into "ephedra-free" herbal weight-loss products by dietary supplement manufacturers.<ref name="nyt">{{cite news |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/10/11/health/policy/11cons.html |title=Bitter Orange Under Scrutiny as New Ephedra |last=Duenwald |first=Mary |date=2005-10-11 |access-date=2008-11-03}}</ref> Bitter orange is believed to cause the same spectrum of [[adverse events]] as ephedra.<ref name="jordan">{{cite journal |last1=Jordan |first1=Scott |last2=Murty |first2=Mano |last3=Pilon |first3=Karen |date=October 2004 |title=Products containing bitter orange or synephrine: suspected == Drug interactions ==

{{see also|Grapefruit–drug interactions}}

Bitter orange may have serious [[Grapefruit–drug interactions|grapefruit-like drug interactions]] with medicines such as [[statin]]s (to lower cholesterol), [[nifedipine]]s (to lower blood pressure), some anti-anxiety drugs, and some antihistamines.<!--this is a few examples, not a list, that's for the linked article which goes into great detail--><ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/grapefruit-juice-and-some-drugs-dont-mix |title=Grapefruit Juice and Some Drugs Don't Mix |journal=FDA |date=14 July 2021 |archive-date=6 May 2019 |access-date=13 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190506062425/https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/grapefruit-juice-and-some-drugs-dont-mix |url-status=live }}</ref>
